title: Mini fridge and 12V cooler: safe teardown
summary: Mini fridges come in three kinds. A thermoelectric (Peltier) cooler gives a 12 V cooling block with heatsinks and fans; a compressor fridge gives a thermostat, start relay, door magnet, glass shelves and an insulated box; a silent absorption minibar gives little but the box. Never cut, drill or heat the sealed refrigerant system: many hold flammable R600a, and absorption units hold ammonia under high pressure.

steps.text: Work out which kind you have before you open anything. Read the rating plate (inside the cabinet or on the back). A compressor fridge names a refrigerant such as R600a or R134a and has a black dome-shaped compressor low at the back. An absorption minibar has no compressor, and its data may list ammonia (NH3) and water (the Dometic RH series table does). A thermoelectric cooler runs on 12 V DC, has a fan grille and finned heatsink, and no refrigerant at all.
steps.warn: R600a and R290 burn. A flammable-refrigerant label or red refrigerant tubing means hydrocarbon gas: keep flames, sparks and cigarettes away for the whole job. Hissing, oily stains or a snapped tube mean the loop is already open: step away, air the room and read safety_refrigerant.

steps.text: Unplug it, or pull the 12 V lead out of its socket, and keep the plug where you can see it. Empty the cabinet. Wait at least 5 minutes before you reach in at the back: the compressor, and the heater block on an absorption unit, can stay hot. A compact fridge or minibar weighs roughly 12 to 20 kg: use two people to pull it from the wall, and keep it upright.

Compressor fridges: once the 5 minutes are up, and before you touch any wiring, deal with the capacitor. At the bottom of the back, take off the cover over the compressor terminals. If there is a capacitor (a small cylinder or block with two terminals), drain it through your resistor tool, holding the probe on each terminal for at least 10 seconds. Only then set the meter to DC volts and measure across the terminals and from each terminal to the chassis; it must read near zero. Clip a jumper wire across the terminals and leave it there while you work (see safety_discharge_capacitor). A run capacitor can hold a mains-level charge after unplugging, so the order is always wait, discharge, then prove, and never bare fingers on the terminals.

Take the door off. Undo the hinge screws (often under a plastic cover on top) and lift the door away. Pull the rubber gasket out of its groove and slit it along its length to get the flexible magnet strip out.
steps.warn: A fridge left with its door on can trap and suffocate a child. Whatever you leave behind, leave it without a door.

steps.text: Lift out the glass shelves and the crisper cover whole. Carry them flat by their faces and stack them with card between.
steps.warn: Shelf glass is usually toughened and bursts into small cubes if an edge is knocked. Wear gloves and eye protection when handling it.

steps.text: Thermostat and light: on some compact fridges they share a housing on the inside ceiling. Undo its screws, lower it, unplug the wires and take the thermostat, its knob and the lamp. A thermostat may have a thin sensing tube that starts at its body and ends clipped or tucked against the cold plate. Unclip it only if it comes freely and you can see where it ends; keep it unkinked. If it runs into foam or won't come, leave the thermostat in place.
steps.warn: Some thin tubes are refrigerant lines and the two can look alike. Never cut, kink or lever on any tube you can't trace back to the thermostat body.

steps.text: Compressor fridges: pull the start relay and overload off the compressor's three pins.
steps.warn: Keep the jumper across the capacitor terminals until the capacitor is out: large capacitors can creep back up to a dangerous voltage.

steps.text: Unplug the capacitor's spade connectors and lift it out, then twist a bare wire across its terminals before you store it. Tape the capacitor, relay and overload together with a note of which fridge they came from: a compressor won't start without its own.

Leave the compressor, the coils and every tube sealed in place. Don't drill, cut or saw into the cabinet walls or back: refrigerant tubing can run hidden inside them. If you need the compressor or coils, look for a unit whose loop is already broken and follow safety_refrigerant. Never cut, drill, unbraze or heat the tubes of an intact one.
steps.warn: A cut line sprays refrigerant and oil: frostbite, eye injury, and fire with R600a. Never use a grinder or torch anywhere near the tubing.

steps.text: Thermoelectric coolers: undo the screws on the back or lid panel to reach the cooling unit. It is a finned heatsink with a fan outside, a smaller heatsink or cold plate inside, and a flat square Peltier module clamped between them. Before you unplug anything from a board, check whether there is a mains supply board inside (some wine coolers and minibars have one). If so, once it has been unplugged for 5 minutes, drain its large capacitors with the resistor tool and prove them empty with the meter (see safety_discharge_capacitor). Then unplug the cooling unit's wires from the control board.

Take the cooling unit out whole. Undo the screws that hold it to the cabinet, not the screws that clamp the two heatsinks together. If you must separate it, loosen the clamping screws a little at a time in a cross pattern.
steps.warn: The module is a brittle ceramic sandwich. Don't pry it with a blade or lift it by its wires. Keep it dry.

steps.text: Take the control board, the power switch, the 12 V car lead and any mains adapter that came with it.
Absorption minibars: take only the door, gasket, shelves, light and controls. Leave the cooling unit at the back exactly as it is, and keep the minibar upright when you move it.
steps.warn: The cooling unit holds ammonia and water under high pressure, and Dometic calls its refrigerant circuit highly flammable. Never open, cut, drill or heat it. If you hear hissing or smell ammonia, go to fresh air, keep flames away and air the room.

steps.text: Keep the cabinet whole. Even dead it is an insulated box: an icebox with ice or cold water jugs, or the body of a new Peltier cooler. Don't burn the foam insulation.
steps.warn: Some cabinet foam is blown with flammable gas. Keep it away from fire.

notes:
## What's worth keeping and why

- **Peltier cooling unit (thermoelectric coolers).** Module, heatsinks and fans as one working block. It runs on 12 V DC: the Koolatron CORC24 car cooler draws about 4.5 A and cools to about 22 °C (40 °F) below the outside air (Koolatron CORC24). Fit it into any insulated box to make a cooler (build_peltier_cooler). Never power the module without a heatsink on its hot side: it overheats, which can burn you and damage the module (Ferrotec precautions). It is power-hungry: the same maker says not to run it for more than 4 hours from a car battery that isn't being charged (Koolatron CORC24).
- **Fans.** Small 12 V DC fans. On a thermoelectric cooler the fan is the only moving part (Koolatron CORC24). Good for ventilation, a solar dehydrator or cooling electronics.
- **Heatsinks.** Finned aluminium blocks for power transistors, LED lamps and voltage regulators.
- **Mains adapter.** Some 12 V coolers come with a 110/120 V adapter: the Koolatron CORC24 does (Koolatron CORC24). Read its label for the output voltage and current before you use it for something else, and don't open it: a mains supply holds large capacitors.
- **Thermostat (compressor fridges).** A mechanical dial switch that turns the compressor on and off. The one in the Danby DCR033B1WM is rated AC 250 V, 6(4) A (Danby DCR033B1WM parts). It can switch a small cooler or a fermentation box. Its range is set for a fridge, so check where it clicks before you rely on it.
- **Start relay, overload and capacitor.** The Danby DCR033B1WM lists a PTC starter, an overload protector and a 6 µF, 250 V CBB65 capacitor beside its compressor (Danby DCR033B1WM parts). Keep them with that compressor; on their own they are small spares.
- **Door magnet.** Danby calls the door seal a magnetic gasket (Danby DAR044A6 manual). The flexible strip inside makes door catches, curtain and screen seals, or a tool holder.
- **Glass shelves.** Usually toughened glass: a solar oven or dehydrator window.
- **Interior light.** The DAR044A6 has an LED light that comes on when the door opens (Danby DAR044A6 manual). Take its door switch too, if it has one.
- **The cabinet.** A ready-made insulated box. The DAR044A6 is 52.7 × 84 × 54.1 cm (20.8 × 33.1 × 21.3 in) outside (Danby DAR044A6 manual). Laid on its back with the door side up it works like a chest cooler, which spills less cold air when opened. If you ever want to run the compressor again, stand it upright for 6 hours first (Danby DAR044A6 manual).
- **Compressor.** Leave it sealed on an intact fridge (see safety_refrigerant). The DCR033B1WM's is a QD3511Y-A rated 110–120 V, 60 Hz, R600a (Danby DCR033B1WM parts).

## Testing what you got out

- **Peltier block:** with the heatsinks and fan still on, connect 12 V for a few seconds. One side should go cold and the other warm. If neither face changes, or it draws no current, the module or its wiring is dead.
- **Fans:** 12 V across the red and black wires; they should spin freely.
- **Thermostat:** on the meter's continuity range, turn the dial from OFF to coldest at room temperature. It should click and show continuity. Set it warm and put the sensing end in a freezer, or in ice with a handful of salt: it should click open (see test_continuity).
- **Capacitor:** see test_capacitor.

## Variations

- **Compressor type.** The common dorm and bar fridge. Both Danby models here use R600a, and Danby warns it is flammable and that the tubing must not be punctured (Danby DAR044A6 manual). The EPA notes that flammable hydrocarbon refrigerant is marked by a warning label and red tubing (EPA disaster guidance). The DAR044A6 defrosts itself into a drip tray above the compressor, where compressor heat dries it (Danby DAR044A6 manual).
- **Thermoelectric type.** 12 V car coolers, some wine coolers and small minibars. No refrigerant (Koolatron CORC24). The Peltier part number and size vary; read the module's label.
- **Absorption type.** Silent hotel minibars. The Dometic RH series runs on 220–240 V, draws 65–75 W, and lists its refrigerant as 147 g of water and 98 g of ammonia. Dometic says never to open the absorber unit because it is under high pressure, that its refrigerant circuit is highly flammable, that the cabinet insulation contains flammable cyclopentane, and to carry the minibar only upright (Dometic RH429LD).

## What to leave

- The sealed system: compressor, condenser, evaporator, the thin capillary tube and the small parts brazed into it. The DCR033B1WM parts list includes a drier filter and a processing tube, both part of that sealed loop (Danby DCR033B1WM parts). See safety_refrigerant.
- The absorption cooling unit, whole and closed.
- Releasing refrigerant on purpose: besides the frostbite and fire risk, in the US it is illegal to knowingly vent most refrigerants when disposing of a fridge (EPA disaster guidance).
- Cabinet foam as fuel: don't burn it.
